CPVC Pipe Problems in Florida Homes: Signs and Solutions

By SRQ Leak Pros Editorial · Published November 5, 2026 · Updated November 5, 2026 · 6 min read

Short answer: The most common CPVC pipe problems are brittleness with age, cracked fittings and failing glued joints. Florida plumbers have reported CPVC snapping when a shut-off valve is turned or a fitting is bumped. Heat and water chemistry may add stress. Handle old CPVC gently, fix leaks fast, and consider a repipe if failures repeat.

CPVC is a rigid plastic pipe used for hot and cold water in many Florida homes. It works well for years, but CPVC pipe problems tend to show up as the pipe ages. A crack inside a wall can soak drywall before anyone notices. If yours keeps failing, SRQ Leak Pros can connect you with a local provider for repiping in Sarasota.

Here's what goes wrong, how to check your pipe and how to decide between repair and repipe.

What is CPVC pipe?

CPVC stands for chlorinated polyvinyl chloride. Wikipedia describes it as PVC that has been chlorinated, which lets it handle higher temperatures than regular PVC. That's why it's used for hot water lines. It's usually cream, tan or light yellow and joined with solvent cement, a glue that fuses the pipe and fitting.

Common CPVC pipe problems

  • Brittleness. Older pipe can crack when bent, bumped or turned.
  • Cracked fittings. Elbows and tees can split, often near a valve.
  • Glued joint failures. Poorly made or aging joints can seep or let go.
  • Valve stress. Turning an old shut-off can snap the pipe behind it.
  • Heat stress. Lines near water heaters or in hot attics age faster.
  • Chemical contact. Some sprays, caulks and fire-stop products can harm CPVC.

What Florida plumbers have reported

In a 2015 WKMG ClickOrlando report, Florida plumbers said CPVC can grow brittle, crack and break over time. They also said the glued joints can break down. Plumbers in the story said Florida heat and chlorine in the water also take a toll. They described CPVC snapping inside a wall when a toilet shut-off valve was turned. One plumber said 40 percent of the homes he had repiped had CPVC.

The report said the manufacturer had cut CPVC's warranty from 25 years to 10, and that it covered the pipe, not water damage. These are reports from working plumbers, not a study. Many CPVC systems work for years without trouble.

Signs your CPVC is failing

  • Leaks at fittings near water heaters or valves
  • Pipe that looks yellowed, darker or chalky
  • Cracks along the pipe or at a joint
  • A snap or crack when you turn a shut-off
  • Repeat leaks in different parts of the house
  • Water stains on ceilings under attic runs

How to inspect your CPVC safely

  1. Find exposed runs. Look under sinks, at the water heater and in the attic or garage.
  2. Look, don't flex. Check for cracks, color change and seeping joints.
  3. Turn valves gently. If an old angle stop won't turn easily, stop. Forcing it can crack the pipe.
  4. Check heat spots. Pay close attention to lines near the water heater.
  5. Note the age. Many owners plan a repipe once failures start repeating.

Repair or repipe?

SituationBetter fit
One cracked fitting, pipe still flexibleSpot repair
Several leaks in a yearRepipe quote
Pipe brittle throughoutRepipe
Cracks near every valve you touchRepipe
Selling a home with known failuresRepair or repipe, and disclose

When a repair is made, a good provider supports the pipe so it doesn't flex. They may also replace nearby angle stops at the same time.

CPVC vs. PEX for a repipe

Many repipes today use PEX. Wikipedia notes PEX is widely used for water supply lines. It's flexible, so it bends around corners with fewer fittings. That means fewer joints that can fail. CPVC is still sold and installed, and some plumbers prefer copper. Ask each bidder what they recommend for your home.

PipeJointsFlexibilityCommon concerns
CPVCSolvent-cement glueRigidBrittleness with age
PEXCrimp or expansion fittingsFlexibleKeep out of sunlight
CopperSoldered or press fittingsRigidPinhole leaks over time

How much does replacing CPVC cost?

Angi's repipe guide, updated July 2026, puts a whole house repipe at about $1,500 to $15,000, with a typical job near $7,500. A partial repipe of one area costs less. See the repipe cost guide for what moves the price.

Florida rules for CPVC repairs and repipes

Florida places water supply work within a plumbing contractor's scope under § 489.105(3)(m). Use a licensed plumbing contractor and check the license on the DBPR site. A full repipe usually needs a permit and inspection.

CPVC in Sarasota homes

Many Sarasota-area homes have supply lines in the attic, where summer heat is intense. CPVC there ages in a harsh spot. Lines near water heaters in garages also face heat. If you own a seasonal home, a small CPVC leak can run for weeks before anyone sees it. Shut the main off when you leave, and have someone check the house.

How to make CPVC last longer

  • Don't hang anything from pipes or step on attic runs.
  • Keep paint, sprays and caulk off the pipe unless rated for CPVC.
  • Support long runs so they don't sag or flex.
  • Replace stiff angle stops with care, using a pro if needed.
  • Keep pressure in a safe range with a working pressure reducing valve.

How to tell if your home has CPVC

Look at exposed pipe under sinks, at the water heater and in the attic. CPVC is usually cream, tan or off-white. The pipe often has printing along its side that names the material. Joints are glued, not crimped or soldered, so you'll see smooth socket fittings with a bead of glue. PEX is flexible and often red, blue or white. Copper is metal. Polybutylene is usually gray and was used in homes from about 1978 to 1997.

If you're not sure, ask a plumber to look. A home inspection report may also name the pipe type.

CPVC when you buy, sell or insure a home

Pipe type can come up during a sale or an insurance review. Keep a record of any CPVC repairs, with dates and locations. If you've had several leaks, a buyer may ask for a repipe quote or a credit. Some insurers ask about pipe type and past leaks, so answer from your records. A repipe invoice and permit can help in both cases.

Local note: many homes in Lakewood Ranch and North Port have plastic supply pipe in hot attics. Seasonal homes on Longboat Key can hide a CPVC leak while owners are away.

Frequently asked questions

How long does CPVC pipe last?

Life varies with heat, water and install quality. Many systems last for years, but brittleness and joint failures tend to rise with age.

Is CPVC still used in Florida?

Yes, CPVC is still sold and installed. Many repipes also use PEX or copper.

Can I fix a cracked CPVC fitting myself?

Small repairs are possible, but old CPVC can crack nearby when handled. Florida treats water supply work as plumbing contractor work.

Does homeowners insurance cover a CPVC leak?

Policies vary. Many cover sudden water damage but not the worn pipe. Read your policy and ask your agent.
